name: NCR
summary:
NCR carries the strongest protective legal framework in the Philippines: Quezon City enacted SP-3417, S-2025, a comprehensive SOGIESC anti-discrimination ordinance, and in July 2025 became the first LGU in the country to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care and specialised services. For a visitor, these represent the only enforceable protections in a country with no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity—complaint routes to a city health office or the QC Gender Desk that simply do not exist elsewhere.

Against that, two of the six documented killings of trans women in the 2024–2025 national series occurred here (Shaina Bayabay strangled in Pasig, March 2024; "Christine" stabbed in Valenzuela, September 2025), and EARIST state college reportedly denied enrollment to trans women requiring short haircuts (March 2024 video). The Commission on Human Rights issued public statements condemning both the campus practice and the killings, and arrests followed in Valenzuela.

Net effect: +0.09 above the national score. The ordinance belt gives a discovered visitor tangible institutional recourse unavailable in sibling regions; the violence, while real, is matched by arrests and official condemnation rather than impunity. Compare Soccsksargen (0.44), where a targeted activist assassination drew the CHR's own "cruelty and impunity" language without comparable protective infrastructure.

name: Central Visayas
summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside Metro Manila. Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024 in formal partnership with the KAABAG LGBT Federation and UNDP—an operational, not merely symbolic, protection framework. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025.

No killings, assaults, or institutional hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents were documented in this region within the 2024–2025 violence series or elsewhere in the dossier.

Net effect: +0.07 above the national score. A visitor in Cebu/Mandaue can file an anti-discrimination complaint under an operational ordinance—the practical equivalent of the NCR protections without the accompanying violence signal. Compare Western Visayas (0.53), which shows the opposite pattern: institutional hostility (Capiz State University campus exclusion) without a compensating protective ordinance.

name: Soccsksargen
summary:
Soccsksargen is the site of the most severe single incident in the national trans-violence series: on 23 June 2025 in General Santos City, a hooded gunman shot Ali Jejhon Macalintal, a transgender rights activist and radio commentator, several times at the acupuncture clinic she owned, killing her; police explicitly investigated whether her history of activism was connected. Human Rights Watch called it an "apparent targeted killing." The Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings as "marked by cruelty and impunity"—the strongest official language in the record, naming Macalintal specifically.

No protective ordinance, institutional counterweight, or positive enforcement response (arrest of the actual gunman) is documented. The "impunity" framing from the CHR is itself the damning signal the scoring rules identify as a large negative factor.

Net effect: −0.12 below the national score. This is the only unit where the violence is both targeted at trans-specificity and explicitly flagged as unaddressed by the official body. Compare NCR (0.65), which carries two killings but pairs them with arrests and the country's strongest protective ordinances; compare Calabarzon (0.51), where a single killing drew a homicide investigation within days.

name: Central Luzon
summary:
Angeles City and the Clark–Subic corridor in Pampanga constitute the region's principal traveler-facing risk. In June 2025 the NBI Bataan District Office dismantled a trafficking ring at Field Sensation's Bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices under the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act, rescuing 12 more victims. Peer-reviewed research describes the US military-basing economy around Clark as sustaining sexual markets that "disproportionately exploit poor transgender Filipina women (trans-Pinays)," and the 2024 US TIP Report confirms traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the environments where trans women are concentrated in sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. There is no protective ordinance cluster here comparable to NCR or Central Visayas.

Net effect: −0.07 below the national score. The trafficking-exposure pattern is structural and documented rather than a single incident. Compare Calabarzon (0.51), which has one killing but no comparable commercial-sex-economy infrastructure drawing visitors into maximum-exposure environments.

name: Calabarzon
summary:
In August 2025 in Lipa City, Batangas, Jericho Elliorante, 25, newly crowned winner of an LGBTQ pageant in Barangay Sambat, Tanauan City, was found with 13 stab wounds. Police opened a homicide case within days of the crowning—a faster institutional response than the unresolved Macalintal shooting in Soccsksargen, but the incident still represents one of the six national killings and occurred in a region with no protective ordinance cluster.

Net effect: −0.05 below the national score. The single-incident rule applies: one killing in eighteen months is not a patterned violence trend for this unit, but the stabbing with 13 wounds and the LGBTQ-pageant context mark it as trans-implicated. The positive element (rapid homicide investigation) prevents a deeper deviation. Compare Cagayan Valley (0.52), whose single killing involved alleged kidnapping and rape—slightly more prolonged violence but also a three-suspect identification within weeks; Calabarzon edges below on the severity of the 13-wound attack.

name: Cagayan Valley
summary:
On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, Morine "G." Cabansag, 40, was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape in Centro San Antonio; three suspects were identified. This is one of the six killings in the 2024–2025 national series. No protective ordinance, institutional hostility finding, or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors was documented in Cagayan Valley beyond this single incident.

Net effect: −0.04 below the national score. The kidnapping-plus-rape-plus-murder sequence is severe in manner, but the rapid identification of three suspects and the absence of any patterned regional signal (compared, for instance, to the commercial sex-economy structure in Central Luzon at 0.49) keep the deviation modest. Compare Soccsksargen (0.44), where the killing was a targeted assassination explicitly condemned by the CHR with the word "impunity" and no protective counterweight.

name: Western Visayas
summary:
In October 2022 the Capiz State University Office of Student Affairs informed students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they conformed on hair and clothing—a documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing in a provincial (not metropolitan) setting. The Alternative Law Groups case study records the subsequent advocacy campaign and a later milestone in reversing the exclusion.

No protective anti-discrimination ordinance comparable to those in Central Visayas or NCR is documented in this region. No killings from the 2024–2025 series occurred here.

Net effect: −0.03 below the national score. The campus exclusion is a climate signal rather than a traveler-facing criminal or facility-exposure risk, and the subsequent reversal by advocacy counts as a good institutional response under the single-incident rule. It sits slightly below national because the episode demonstrates that in a conservative provincial setting, expression can be policed by institutional authority without legal recourse, and the region lacks the protective-ordinance belt present in Central Visayas (0.63).

name: Ilocos Region
summary:
The Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of Bayambang protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons (Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, session of 19 August 2024)—a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal LGBTQ+ protection ordinance in a conservative province. This gives a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor a local complaint route absent in most other regions.

Against that, the Abra and Ilocos Sur provinces within Ilocos Region host the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group (BIAG), a codified customary-justice system with its own dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences," recognised by Philippine courts. No trans-specific bodong ruling or customary exclusion was documented, but the legal-pluralism structure means that in a rural Abra or Ilocos Sur dispute, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

Net effect: +0.03 above the national score, modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the plural-justice uncertainty is localized to specific provinces within the region. Compare Central Visayas (0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city IRRs with UNDP backing, unanimous municipal votes) and there is no countervailing alternative-justice structure.

name: ARMM
summary:
ARMM (predecessor to BARMM) is the only unit where a structurally different legal system applies to a visitor in conflict situations. The Bangsamoro Administrative Code (BAA-13, 2019) provides that justice in the autonomous region shall be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws." Parliament Bill No. 473 (July 2026) proposes a comprehensive Bangsamoro Shari'ah Justice System Code adding ta'zir criminal offences—the category under which morality offences against same-sex conduct and gender expression are prosecuted in comparable systems. Nationally, the Shari'ah court system is expanding: President Marcos Jr. signed a law in August 2024 creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts beyond BARMM, RA 12304 (September 2025) ensures equitable access, and the Supreme Court resolved in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.

The dossier's assessor caveat is explicit: no source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and the original P.D. 1083 codified only personal law. The finding is structural—a jurisdiction with an active legislative process to create criminal religious law, in a region where a visitor's dispute may be adjudicated outside the Philippine court system entirely—rather than a documented enforcement reality.

Net effect: −0.07 below the national score. The risk is forward-looking and legal-framework-based, not enforcement-based, which limits the deviation under the "enforcement > statute" rule. However, the ta'zir drafting is the single most severe structural threat identified in the dossier for a transgender visitor, and the absence of any protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure in ARMM means no counterweight exists. Compare CAR (0.54), which also has a legal-pluralism concern but no criminal-law component.

name: CAR
summary:
The Kalinga bodong/pagta system—bilateral inter-tribal peace pacts with their own holders, sanctions and dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences"—was formally codified by the Kalinga provincial government in February 2026 as a 137-page written Pagta. Philippine courts recognise the bodong; academic literature frames it as legal pluralism in which indigenous and formal criminal justice coexist, with police handling customary-law cases. For a visitor whose dispute falls under a bodong's jurisdiction, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

No trans-specific bodong ruling, customary exclusion, or gender-expression punishment was documented in the dossier. The constitutional recognition of indigenous justice also appears in the Bangsamoro Basic Law's IP-rights section, reinforcing the framework.

Net effect: −0.02 below the national score. The finding is a structural uncertainty (which court applies to you) without any evidence of trans-specific adverse outcome. It sits at the threshold of the minimum deviation. Compare ARMM (0.49), where the legal-pluralism concern is paired with an active criminal-law drafting process (ta'zir offences) that raises the stakes materially; here the bodong is a civil/ADR institution with no criminal-law expansion documented for morality offences.
